item.aggregated_output:
<<2:40 update 1, part 0 of 0..2>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
2:40/q01 Who are the Children of Israel? [يَٰبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · referent]
  2:40/q01/p1 Jacob's descendants, named for Jacob son of Isaac son of Abraham. — reasons: Tabari compares Children of Adam; the Prophet elicited Jewish confirmation that Israel is Jacob; Abu Hayyan and Biqai stress ancestral honor.
2:40/q02 What does the name Israel mean? [إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · meaning] (turns on: The reported Hebrew and narrative derivations differ.)
  2:40/q02/p1 Servant of God, equivalent to Abd Allah. — reasons: Ibn Abbas parses Isra as servant and El as God; Abdullah ibn al-Harith confirms El; angelic names are compared.
  2:40/q02/p2 God's chosen one. — reasons: Tha'labi, Kashshaf and others report the Hebrew derivation; Abu Hayyan attributes it to Ibn Abbas and others.
  2:40/q02/p3 One whom God strengthened or firmly formed. — reasons: Al-Mahdawi derives Isra from strength; Kur'an Yolu finds this probable; Abu Hayyan calls popular etymologies weak.
  2:40/q02/p4 Man of God. — reasons: Al-Qaffal says Hebrew Isra means human.
  2:40/q02/p5 Night migrant toward God. — reasons: Al-Suhayli and other accounts connect the name to Jacob's night migration; Abu Hayyan questions popular etymologies.
  2:40/q02/p6 Other proposed meanings include God's sword and one striving in God's path. — reasons: Kur'an Yolu reports these.
2:40/q03 Who is addressed by this call? [يَٰبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · referent] (turns on: Whether ancestral favors count for unbelieving descendants.)
  2:40/q03/p1 Jews of Muhammad's time, especially scholars in and around Medina. — reasons: Ibn Abbas and the majority identify Jewish scholars; Bursevi names Qurayza and Nadir; Ibn Atiyya includes believers and unbelievers.
  2:40/q03/p2 Jews and Christians, the People of Scripture. — reasons: Jishumi reports Abu Ali; Tabrisi and Abu Hayyan link the address to the general call and Adam story.
  2:40/q03/p3 Only Israelites who believed in Muhammad. — reasons: Makki argues unbelievers cannot receive favor; Ibn Atiyya notes the direct address then calls for continued commitment.
  2:40/q03/p4 All descendants or accountable people generally. — reasons: Jishumi reports a general reading; Abu Hayyan extends the duties to everyone.
2:40/q04 Why call them by Israel's name? [يَٰبَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · rhetoric]
  2:40/q04/p1 It honors a righteous ancestor and urges obedience to his faith. — reasons: Abu Hayyan cites attachment to ancestors (43:22; 2:170); Burhan compares sons of Abdullah; Alusi says conduct matters more in a prophetic family.
  2:40/q04/p2 The vocative draws attention to the ensuing commands. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya calls ya attention getting; Abu Hayyan compares 2:21 and 2:35.
2:40/q05 How is Banī Isrāʾīl formed grammatically? [بَنِىٓ إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · grammar] (turns on: The disputed lost radical and range of collective descent.)
  2:40/q05/p1 Banī is an accusative construct vocative; Israel is genitive in position but diptote. — reasons: Zajjaj supplies implicit 'I call'; Nahhas notes deleted nūn and accusative yā; Ibn Atiyya cites al-Khalil and Abu Ali; the plural can take feminine agreement.
  2:40/q05/p2 Ibn derives from yā connected to building. — reasons: Zajjaj, Abu Ishaq and Jawhari prefer this; the father is the foundation and the son a branch. Fatūwa answers the banūwa objection.
  2:40/q05/p3 Ibn derives from wāw. — reasons: Al-Akhfash cites banūwa and more frequent deletion of wāw; Nahhas, Samin and Alusi dispute those grounds.
  2:40/q05/p4 The plural title includes women as well as men. — reasons: Alusi says ibn literally denotes male sons but the construct commonly covers all descendants; al-Salikuti calls this figurative. Alusi notes prohibited metaphorical divine sonship.
2:40/q06 How is Israel pronounced or read? [إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · readings] (turns on: Transmitted pronunciations of a foreign proper name differ.)
  2:40/q06/p1 The common form has long alif, hamza and yāʾ. — reasons: Jishumi, Tabrisi and Samin call it eloquent; Abu Hayyan and Alusi attribute it to the majority; foreign words admit Arabic alteration.
  2:40/q06/p2 Forms omit or ease hamza with varying length. — reasons: Reports name Hasan, Zuhri, Abu Ja'far, Nafi', A'mash, Isa, Warsh and Ibn Abi Ishaq. Saffar questions deletion of initial hamza.
  2:40/q06/p3 Forms omit yā or replace lām with nūn. — reasons: Tamimi Isra'in has poetic and phonological parallels; Umayya attests Isral; imāla is also transmitted.
2:40/q07 What accounts explain Jacob's name and history? [إِسْرَٰٓءِيلَ · reports] (turns on: The narratives and counts differ.)
  2:40/q07/p1 Jacob wrestled an angel and was named Israel. — reasons: Abu Majliz says Jacob seized the angel and demanded a name; Durr adds a blow to his thighs and calls it an angelic name.
  2:40/q07/p2 Jacob captured a jinn called Il that extinguished Temple lamps. — reasons: Ka'b describes Jacob's Temple service; Samin mentions a mixed-language name.
  2:40/q07/p3 Jacob and Esau's rivalry, Isaac's blessings and Jacob's flight are recounted. — reasons: Tha'labi reports the twins' birth, Rebecca's disguise, blessings and Esau's threat; Abu Hayyan mentions night migration to their uncle.
  2:40/q07/p4 Reports differ over prophets with two names. — reasons: Ibn al-Jawzi singles out Jacob besides Muhammad; al-Khalil lists five pairs; an Ibn Abbas report singles out Israel and Jesus; Jawhari calls Messiah underived.
2:40/q08 What does 'remember' ask them to do? [ٱذْكُرُوا۟ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether recollection alone or gratitude is intended.)
  2:40/q08/p1 Preserve the favor in heart and memory, without forgetting. — reasons: Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya oppose recollection to forgetting; Qurtubi regards inward retention as a good explanation.
  2:40/q08/p2 Give thanks, praise and obey the Giver. — reasons: Baghawi transmits Hasan; Kashshaf requires recognition, magnification and obedience; Ibn Jawzi says memory without gratitude is incomplete; Wahidi identifies belief in Muhammad as required gratitude.
  2:40/q08/p3 Bring something to attention by heart or tongue. — reasons: Jishumi and Tabrisi list honor, scripture, prayer and speech among dhikr's uses; Harali defines recalling what was forgotten.
2:40/q09 How do the forms and senses of dhikr differ? [ٱذْكُرُوا۟ · meaning]
  2:40/q09/p1 Heart remembrance and spoken mention differ by vowel or are synonymous. — reasons: Al-Kisai assigns damma to heart and kasra to speech; others treat both alike; Alusi weighs homonymy against a shared general sense.
  2:40/q09/p2 The imperative derives from the remembrance verb. — reasons: Nahhas explains deletion of nūn and connecting alif and initial damma; Farra equates a form with tadhakkaru; Baydawi reports udhkuru and idhtakiru.
2:40/q10 What does niʿmah mean? [نِعْمَتِىَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether a benefit's ultimate outcome affects its name.)
  2:40/q10/p1 A bestowed benefit intended kindly. — reasons: Damghani and Ibn Jawzi gloss favor; Jishumi requires good intent; Razi excludes pure harm, self-serving help and poisoned gifts; Harali includes bodily and spiritual suitability.
  2:40/q10/p2 All benefits ultimately come from God. — reasons: Razi cites 16:53 and 31:14: God creates intermediaries, capacity, motive and guidance; people may still be thanked, as a hadith says.
  2:40/q10/p3 Worldly benefits bless even disbelievers. — reasons: Razi prefers Baqillani, citing creation, provision, rescue, security and prosperity; the dispute is partly terminological.
  2:40/q10/p4 Worldly benefits that end in eternal harm are not blessings to disbelievers. — reasons: Some Sunnis compare them to poisoned sweets and cite 3:178.
  2:40/q10/p5 All accountable people receive equal religious aid; some also require the best worldly aid. — reasons: Razi attributes the latter to Baghdadi Mu'tazilites, not Basrans; Sunnis say God creates both benefits and harms.
2:40/q11 Which favor or favors are recalled? [نِعْمَتِىَ ٱلَّتِىٓ أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ · referent] (turns on: Whether examples restrict the unspecified favor.)
  2:40/q11/p1 Israel's many historic favors, including favors to ancestors. — reasons: Sources enumerate rescue from Pharaoh, the parted sea, land, prophets, books, manna, quails, shade, springs, pardon and Torah. Ibn Abbas adds nighttime light, unworn clothes and untangled hair; 5:20 is a parallel.
  2:40/q11/p2 The Torah's knowledge of Muhammad and life in his era. — reasons: Ibn al-Anbari says failing to follow him is like forgetting entrusted knowledge; Kashshaf and Nasafi count reaching his time as favor; Elmali emphasizes guidance.
  2:40/q11/p3 All favors, beginning with creation, faculties and Islam. — reasons: Ibn Zayd calls Islam greatest (49:17); Jishumi and Tabrisi include reason, senses, provision and protection; Ibn Atiyya prefers the generic word over restricted examples.
2:40/q12 Why can singular niʿmah mean many favors? [نِعْمَتِىَ · grammar]
  2:40/q12/p1 It is a generic or collective singular. — reasons: Tha'labi, Jishumi, Baghawi, Tabrisi and others cite 14:34 or 16:18; Ibn Jawzi compares Arabic singulars used collectively.
2:40/q13 How do favors to ancestors count for descendants? [أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ · rhetoric] (turns on: Ancestral benefit and the motive for direct address.)
  2:40/q13/p1 Descendants inherit ancestral benefit and honor. — reasons: Zajjaj cites Arabic attribution of forebears' deeds to descendants; Razi adds existence itself; Alusi invokes shared religious inheritance.
  2:40/q13/p2 Naming their own favor encourages gratitude over envy. — reasons: Baydawi, Bursevi and Alusi note that people readily value their own gifts; attribution to God directs gratitude to Him.
  2:40/q13/p3 Recalling past gifts raises hope for future favor. — reasons: Razi says a repeated benefactor is expected to continue kindness, restraining opposition.
2:40/q14 How is the yāʾ of niʿmatī read? [نِعْمَتِىَ · readings] (turns on: Resolution of yāʾ before connecting alif.)
  2:40/q14/p1 Vowel it with fatḥa before
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<2:40 update 1, part 1 of 0..2>>
 the article. — reasons: Farra, Akhfash, Zajjaj, Tabrisi and Ibn Atiyya prefer preserving the letter and avoiding two silent letters; Abu Hayyan and Alusi say the seven readers agree.
  2:40/q14/p2 Leave it still, dropping it where two sukūns meet. — reasons: Farra permits this before alif-lam and discusses hamza contexts and 39:53/17; Baydawi notes a pause/connection practice.
2:40/q15 How is the yāʾ of biʿahdī read? [بِعَهْدِىٓ · readings]
  2:40/q15/p1 It remains quiescent before the following alif. — reasons: Ibn Mujahid records unmoved forms, Nafi's general vocalization rule and exceptions, Ibn Jammaz and Ismail ibn Ja'far's still yāʾ; Nashr says readers agree here because of the many letters.
2:40/q16 How is the relative phrase constructed? [ٱلَّتِىٓ أَنْعَمْتُ عَلَيْكُمْ · grammar]
  2:40/q16/p1 Allatī modifies niʿmah; the relative clause omits a resumptive object. — reasons: Nahhas, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi supply 'I bestowed it'; Samin cites a 9:69 reading for deletion after preposition loss.
  2:40/q16/p2 The clause clarifies and widens the favor. — reasons: Harali interprets allatī as initially vague; Samin says ʿalaykum conveys comprehensive reach.
2:40/q17 What does ʿahd mean? [بِعَهْدِىٓ بِعَهْدِكُمْ · meaning]
  2:40/q17/p1 A pledge, testament or undertaking to preserve and fulfill. — reasons: Mawardi cites scripture and oath; Jishumi says command/testament; Tabatabai derives preservation; Biqai's Harali, Isfahani and Khalil describe prior private undertaking and continual tending; Kur'an Yolu lists compact, promise and oath.
  2:40/q17/p2 It can name the Mosaic law and the many divine duties. — reasons: Ibn Ashur notes Israel's scripture uses covenant for law; Kur'an Yolu relates Old and New Testaments to covenant obligations.
2:40/q18 What covenant must Israel fulfill? [وَأَوْفُوا۟ بِعَهْدِىٓ · interpretation] (turns on: Unspecified covenant: all obligations or a specific historical or inward pledge.)
  2:40/q18/p1 All commands, prohibitions, faith and obedience, including Muhammad. — reasons: Ibn Abbas and the majority give the broad view. Ibn Ashur cites 5:12-13, 5:70-71, 2:84-85 and Jewish scriptures: worship, prayer, alms, support for messengers, no bloodshed and fidelity to all revelation.
  2:40/q18/p2 Believe and follow Muhammad as foretold, disclosing his description. — reasons: Tabari cites 5:12 and 7:157; Kalbi reports the unlettered prophet of Ishmael's line with double reward; Zajjaj cites 3:187; Kashshaf points to 2:41. Razi debates explicitness and concealment.
  2:40/q18/p3 Keep the specific 5:12 pledge with twelve chiefs. — reasons: It requires prayer, alms, belief in messengers and a good loan; it promises forgiveness and gardens. Muqatil, Qatada, Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj identify it.
  2:40/q18/p4 Hold fast to Torah under the Sinai pledge. — reasons: Hasan links it to the raised mountain and 2:63; others cite 2:93.
  2:40/q18/p5 Worship God alone and follow Islam. — reasons: Abu al-Aliya calls the covenant Islam; Muqatil and Thalabi cite 2:83.
  2:40/q18/p6 Thank God for disclosed favors. — reasons: Tabrisi and Razi report that disclosure binds them to gratitude; Study Quran generalizes it.
  2:40/q18/p7 Do not flee battle. — reasons: Ismail ibn Ziyad cites 8:15-16 and 33:15; Abu Hayyan adds Paradise as reward.
  2:40/q18/p8 Keep the primordial pledge of assent and service. — reasons: Sulami's Baghdadis and Bursevi recall pretemporal assent; Qushayri pairs acceptance with fulfillment at return.
  2:40/q18/p9 Guard trusts, secrets, manners, self, reliance and sincerity inwardly. — reasons: Sulami gives distinct reciprocal pairs: trusts/treasuries, duties/acceptance, struggle/help, manners/adornment, reliance/sufficiency, worship/stations, service/vision. Qushayri and Abu Hayyan add knowledge, love, contentment and proximity; Qurtubi reports such readings.
2:40/q19 What does God promise in return? [أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: The promised outcome varies with the proposed human commitment.)
  2:40/q19/p1 Acceptance, forgiveness, reward and Paradise. — reasons: Muqatil and Tabari cite 5:12; Ibn Abbas adds divine pleasure; Qurtubi says obedience signals rather than causes gracious reward; a Prophetic report promises Paradise.
  2:40/q19/p2 Lift burdens and fetters when Israel follows Muhammad. — reasons: Ibn Abbas says prior burdens followed sins; Tabari, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir and Elmali link release to prophetic belief.
  2:40/q19/p3 Give double reward to People of Scripture who follow earlier prophets and Muhammad. — reasons: Kalbi transmits forgiveness, Paradise and two rewards; Razi cites 28:52-54, 57:28 and a hadith on three double-reward groups.
  2:40/q19/p4 Give worldly security, sufficiency and victory. — reasons: Biqai cites Torah language of livelihood and freedom from fear; Elmali relates 2:38; Sulami and Qushayri pair reliance with sufficiency.
  2:40/q19/p5 Give inward help, nearness, vision and communion. — reasons: Sulami, Qushayri, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Alusi describe levels from confession and protection to unity and encounter.
2:40/q20 How are the two covenants annexed? [بِعَهْدِىٓ بِعَهْدِكُمْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether annexation names maker or beneficiary, and whether the promise is causal.)
  2:40/q20/p1 Either party may be named as maker or beneficiary. — reasons: Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan and Samin discuss subject/object annexation; Baydawi and Alusi prefer God's initiating command and promised reward; Alusi notes a caveat to both as object genitives.
  2:40/q20/p2 Reciprocal language expresses command and promised reward. — reasons: Razi says God cannot be commanded, so divine 'covenant' differs from human obligation, as in reciprocal plotting/deceiving language.
  2:40/q20/p3 Human fulfillment signals, rather than causes, God's gracious act. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Qurtubi reject a causal obligation upon God.
2:40/q21 What do awfū and awfi mean? [وَأَوْفُوا۟ أُوفِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether doubling intensifies or simply varies the form.)
  2:40/q21/p1 Awfā, wafā and waffā can all mean fulfilling a covenant. — reasons: Zajjaj prefers Qur'anic awfā; Ibn Awf's verse combines forms; Farra distinguishes Hijaz and Najd; Ibn Qutayba allows both for covenants but only awfā for fully measuring; Abu al-Haytham rejects Shammar's distinction.
  2:40/q21/p2 Awfā can also mean rise or ascend. — reasons: Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi cite a poem; Shammar distinguishes rights fully paid from mere completion.
  2:40/q21/p3 A doubled verb can intensify repeated or abundant fulfillment. — reasons: Ibn Jinni says doubled form is emphatic, comparing 6:160, while his light-form discussion of yudhabbihun says a generic verbal noun may itself indicate repeated action; he cites Arabic poets and morphological variation.
  2:40/q21/p4 The doubled form can be simply synonymous. — reasons: Abu Hayyan and Tha'labi permit that account.
2:40/q22 Which doubled fulfillment reading is transmitted? [وَأَوْفُوا۟ بِعَهْدِىٓ أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ · readings] (turns on: Transmission and morphological force.)
  2:40/q22/p1 Al-Zuhrī reads doubled fāʾ, sometimes in both clauses. — reasons: Nahhas, Ibn Jinni and later writers report it, differing on the first clause and vowel detail; Baydawi reports a doubled wāw.
  2:40/q22/p2 The common light form remains the basis of comparison. — reasons: The doubled form can imply amplification rather than a new obligation.
2:40/q23 Why is awfi jussive? [وَأَوْفُوا۟ بِعَهْدِىٓ أُوفِ بِعَهْدِكُمْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the command or an elided condition governs.)
  2:40/q23/p1 The imperative itself carries conditional force and licenses the response. — reasons: Nahhas and al-Khalil describe it; Abu al-Hasan ibn Khuruf and one Sibawayh account support direct licensing.
  2:40/q23/p2 An elided if-clause governs the jussive. — reasons: Al-Farisi and al-Sirafi supply 'if you fulfill'; Abu Hayyan reports Sibawayh citing al-Khalil for this account.
2:40/q24 What does rahbah mean? [فَٱرْهَبُونِ · meaning] (turns on: Whether caution is intrinsic to rahbah.)
  2:40/q24/p1 Fear, dread or apprehension, often with caution. — reasons: Jishumi cites the fear/mercy proverb; Tabrisi contrasts desire; Abu Hayyan records vocalizations and a breastbone derivation; Baydawi and Alusi distinguish wary fear from taqwa.
  2:40/q24/p2 Fear rests on belief about harm and benefit. — reasons: Jishumi says perceived harm prompts avoidance and perceived benefit prompts action.
2:40/q25 What are they to fear? [وَإِيَّٰىَ فَٱرْهَبُونِ · interpretation] (turns on: The feared consequence and scope of the immediate covenant.)
  2:40/q25/p1 God alone, especially when breaking covenant or denying Muhammad. — reasons: Muqatil warns of Hell for denial; Tabari warns of punishment unless they repent; Wahidi, Baghawi and Tabrisi focus on breach; Baydawi and Alusi extend fear to all deeds.
  2:40/q25/p2 Ancestral calamities, including transformation. — reasons: Ibn Abbas' warning recurs in Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir and Alusi.
  2:40/q25/p3 Future punishment under certain or uncertain accountability. — reasons: Razi says prophets and angels may fear the future (16:50); uncertainty about past obedience creates further fear.
  2:40/q25/p4 Fear rabbis no more; follow the promised messenger. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says leaders obstructed covenant keeping; Elmali distinguishes common people and elites in 2:40-41.
2:40/q26 What force does fronting Me add? [وَإِيَّٰىَ فَٱرْهَبُونِ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether fronting alone suffices or the combined construction does.)
  2:40/q26/p1 It intensifies exclusive fear of God. — reasons: Kashshaf compares 1:5; Baydawi cites fronting and repeated object; Alusi adds fa and implied condition; Ibn Ashur details four ascending emphases and cites feared leaders; Qushayri invokes God's sole creative power.
  2:40/q26/p2 Fronting alone does not always restrict. — reasons: Abu Hayyan rejects Zamakhshari's stated

basis; Ibn Ashur rejects Sakkaki's placement account and cites Zuhayr for a nonexclusive example.
  2:40/q26/p3 The exclusivity extends to hope and divine decree. — reasons: Razi argues independent human action would require fearing others and oneself.
2:40/q27 What governs iyyāya? [وَإِيَّٰىَ فَٱرْهَبُونِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the governor is elided, spoken after rearrangement, or nominal.)
  2:40/q27/p1 An elided imperative governs the detached accusative. — reasons: Zajjaj, Wahidi, Jishumi and others say the overt verb already has its attached object; Samin prefers a postposed estimate; Burhan places this in the general elided-governor category and compares other constructions.
  2:40/q27/p2 The construction may be nominal or governed by the overt verb after rearrangement. — reasons: Qurtubi allows an understood 'I am your Lord'; Abu Hayyan and Samin derive an attention-command structure with object repetition.
  2:40/q27/p3 A raised-topic analysis supplies omitted predication. — reasons: Tabrisi compares Sibawayh's verse and 5:38 and 24:2.
2:40/q28 What does fa do in fa-rhabūn? [فَٱرْهَبُونِ · grammar] (turns on: Whether fa is conditional, coordinate or pleonastic.)
  2:40/q28/p1 It marks an implied condition: if anything is feared, fear Me. — reasons: Baydawi and Bursevi make it explicit; Ibn Ashur calls it universal and cites 74:3; Abu Hayyan discusses an elided attention command.
  2:40/q28/p2 It coordinates an elided command with the overt command. — reasons: Al-Miftah proposes continued or heightened fear; Alusi objects to simple coordination of two particles but admits a refined elliptical account; later scholars prefer it.
  2:40/q28/p3 It is extra. — reasons: Samin reports this analysis.
2:40/q29 How is the final yāʾ read? [فَٱرْهَبُونِ · readings] (turns on: Codex spelling, pause practice, dialect and transmission.)
  2:40/q29/p1 Most omit it at verse end, even in connection. — reasons: Zajjaj and Wahidi cite cadence; Jishumi cites codex and ease; Ibn Ashur invokes Hudhayl dialect, pause treatment and Sibawayh; Tabrisi notes nūn kasra.
  2:40/q29/p2 Yaʿqūb and some others retain it. — reasons: Nahhas and Ibn Atiyya name Ibn Abi Ishaq; Tabrisi names Ibn Kathir in connection; Nashr and Ibn Ashur report Ya'qub in pause and connection, matching Hijazi usage.
2:40/q30 What inward meanings are given to fear? [وَإِيَّٰىَ فَٱرْهَبُونِ · inward] (turns on: Punishment, thoughts or divine majesty as the object.)
  2:40/q30/p1 Fear is inner light and certainty reached by striving. — reasons: Tustari joins piety, tawhid, heart sight and trust; nearness excludes indwelling or union; certainty affects the Resurrection scale.
  2:40/q30/p2 Awe guards the heart's thoughts and belongs to knowledge. — reasons: Sulami defines inner apprehension; Sahl contrasts awe in certainty with piety under divine stratagem.
  2:40/q30/p3 Punishment fear is temporary; awe of majesty endures. — reasons: Razi's gnostics, Abu Hayyan and Alusi distinguish outward practitioners and people of the heart.
  2:40/q30/p4 Fear now brings security on Judgment Day. — reasons: Razi reports the saying that God does not combine two fears or securities; greater present fear yields greater future safety.
2:40/q31 What obligations and theological principles does the verse establish? [* · theology] (turns on: The basis of reciprocal promise and human duty.)
  2:40/q31/p1 Gratitude, covenant fidelity and fear are duties. — reasons: Tabrisi calls concealing favor a grave sin; Razi says favor and prior pledge aggravate breach; Baydawi and Bursevi summarize promise and threat.
  2:40/q31/p2 Human acts are real. — reasons: Tabrisi argues denial would void covenant, command, promise, threat, messenger and scripture.
  2:40/q31/p3 God's promised reward must occur because His report is truthful. — reasons: Razi rejects Mu'tazili rational indebtedness and his Ash'ari school's bare denial as complete accounts, preferring truthful promise.
  2:40/q31/p4 Only God deserves praise and fear as creator. — reasons: Razi says idols cannot benefit or harm (26:72-73 etc); Qushayri says a powerless being is not feared.
  2:40/q31/p5 Muhammad's mission addresses Israelites too. — reasons: Razi draws this from the passage; Ibn Kathir calls them to Islam.
2:40/q32 How does the address fit the surrounding passage? [* · links] (turns on: How the universal call gives way to ancestral history.)
  2:40/q32/p1 It turns from general proofs and Adam to Israel's favors and duties. — reasons: Tabari says Jewish knowledge of ancestral reports confirms revelation; Razi charts invitation, inducement, warning and detailed favors; Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan, Alusi and Kur'an Yolu explain the turn to the People of Scripture. Tabatabai counts twelve episodes of rescue, Sinai, calf, thunderbolt and revival, showing care despite ingratitude.
  2:40/q32/p2 Israel is led from favor to Benefactor; Muhammad's community from Benefactor to favor. — reasons: Sulami, Razi, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Bursevi compare 2:152.
  2:40/q32/p3 It pairs encouragement with warning and closes in submission. — reasons: Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan describe the sequence of promise, faith, bodily/financial duties and final fear.
2:40/q33 What earlier-scripture evidence points to Muhammad? [وَأَوْفُوا۟ بِعَهْدِىٓ · links] (turns on: How explicit and identifiable the predictions were.)
  2:40/q33/p1 Prior scriptures are read as promising Muhammad. — reasons: Razi adduces Deuteronomy's prophet from Israel's brothers, Paran, Habakkuk, Isaiah's city, Ishmael's great nation, Abraham's prayer, Jesus' Ahmad and Paraclete announcements, and Daniel's stone kingdom. He replies to objections about 'among you,' Paran as fire, Jerusalem and the Messiah; Ibn Razin and Christian transmissions give variants.
  2:40/q33/p2 The predictions may have been obscure or known only to a few. — reasons: Razi says explicit public time and place would be hard to hide, prompting some to favor a general covenant; defenders say the details were not universally plain.
